(CNN) -- Despite the obvious claims of younger rivals Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi, few can really argue with the 96 football journalists who voted Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite as the 2007 World Footballer of the Year. Brazilian genius Kaka fully deserves winning the 2007 World Footballer of the Year award. The prestigious Ballon d'Or award is widely regarded as the most prestigious individual prize in football and Kaka's inclusion on its coveted roll of honor is a testament to the 25-year-old Brazilian's current standing in world football. When AC Milan defeated Liverpool in the Champions League final in Athens, avenging their heartbreaking loss to the same team in Istanbul two years previously, it enabled Kaka to fulfill his dream of holding aloft Europe's premier trophy -- a winner's medal he fully deserved after a sublime 90-minute performance. Kaka's stock for both club and country has risen steadily since his move to the San Siro from Sao Paulo for a fee of just $8.5 million in the summer of 2003. Unlike many a Brazilian sporting genius, Kaka did not hone his skills on the beach or the streets of a favela shanty town. He was born into a comfortable middle class Brasilia family, where football was not the only hope of a bright future. However, it soon became clear that this particular boy had a very special skill and he was signed by Sao Paulo, after his family had moved there, at just eight years of age -- making his first team debut as an 18-year-old. Kaka's progress was soon picked up by his national team coach and Felipe Scolari named the graceful midfielder in his 23-man squad for the 2002 World Cup finals, earning him a winners' medal despite playing only 19 minutes of the tournament in a group match against Costa Rica. A year later, and Kaka was on his way to Milan. Within a month he had made the starting line-up and his 10 goals helped the Rossoneri lift the Scudetto and the European Super Cup. Throughout his career, Kaka has always possessed the innate ability to score goals -- his record for both club and country sees him average roughly a goal every three games. Yet to describe Kaka merely as a goalscoring midfielder would be doing him a massive injustice. Tall, elegant and blessed with astonishing skill, Milan and Brazil utilize Kaka's ability superbly. Milan coach Carlo Ancelotti soon recognized Kaka's genius, changing his team's system to a 4-4-1-1, playing the Brazilian behind a main target man. With Andrea Pirlo and Gennaro Gattuso holding the central midfield area, Kaka has a license to roam in behind the lone striker, be it Filippo Inzaghi, Ronaldo or Alberto Gilardino. And Kaka does this with devastating effect, running at the opposition with pace and power, finding defense-splitting passes or shooting from range with deadly accuracy be it from a dead-ball situation or open play. The fly in the ointment for Milan comes in the shape of their poor form this season. Although they have already reached the last 16 of the Champions League, the club are floundering in Serie A and face the unthinkable prospect of not qualifying for next season's competition unless they win the trophy. Real Madrid have coveted Kaka for the last two years -- expect the world transfer record to be smashed if Milan don't secure a place among Europe's elite. E-mail to a friend .

**Brazil's Kaka named FIFA World Player of the Year**

December 17, 2007 
From CNN Sports

**ZURICH, Switzerland (CNN)** -- AC Milan midfielder Kaka was crowned FIFA World Player of the Year on Monday, completing a clean sweep of football's top individual honors for 2007 after beating out Barcelona's Lionel Messi and Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo.

The 25-year-old Brazilian received 1,047 votes from the head coaches and captains of international teams, finishing comfortably ahead of the 20-year-old Messi (504 votes) and 22-year-old Ronaldo (426 votes) at a star-studded gala held at the Zurich Opera House.

The award tops off an extraordinary 12 months for the playmaker, whose full name is Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite. Kaka was the driving force behind AC Milan's seventh European Cup triumph in May, finishing as the UEFA Champions League's top scorer with 10 goals. 

Monday's coronation came just 24 hours after Kaka helped Milan lift the FIFA Club World Cup in Yokohama, Japan, where he scored once and set up two goals in a 4-2 victory over Argentine side Boca Juniors.

"Tonight is a very special night for me," Kaka said after receiving the trophy. "When I was young, I just dreamed of playing for Sao Paulo and playing one game for the national team. That was it. But the Bible says that God gives us more than we ask for, and that is what has happened in my life."

Kaka's landslide victory follows his winning of the prestigious Ballon d'Or (European Footballer of the Year) earlier this month. He becomes the fifth Brazilian to win the FIFA award since its inception in 1991, joining Romario, Rivaldo, Ronaldo, and Ronaldinho.

Runner-up Messi was recognized for a sensational year in Spain, highlighted by a famous hat-trick against Real Madrid and a stunning individual goal against Getafe that drew comparisons to Diego Maradona. Ronaldo earned third place after inspiring Manchester United to their first English Premier League title in four years with 23 goals in all competitions. 

It was a night of double celebration for Brazilian football, as 21-year-old forward Marta was named FIFA Women's World Player of the Year for the second consecutive year. Marta was the top scorer and player of the tournament at the Women's World Cup in China, where Brazil finished as runners-up to Germany.

With the world's most coveted individual trophy now in hand, Kaka insisted his focus remains on collective success with both Milan and the Brazilian national team as they look ahead to 2008.

"A new era has begun in football, but for me, the goal remains the same," Kaka told reporters. "To keep winning trophies with my team."

**PARIS —** In an era where global sports icons are increasingly crafted in the fires of extreme adversity or hyper-commercialized academies, Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite stands as a brilliant, serene anomaly. 

To the world, he is simply Kaká. And on Sunday evening in Paris, clad in a tailored black suit with a smile that could light up the San Siro, the 25-year-old Brazilian officially stood atop the footballing pantheon, collecting the 2007 Ballon d’Or as the undisputed best player on the planet.

Kaká’s victory—surpassing two prodigies named Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi in the voting—feels less like the start of a routine reign and more like the crowning of footballing royalty. Yet, the story of how this devout, polite young man became the undisputed king of Europe’s most demanding sport subverts almost every trope of the modern Brazilian superstar.

### The Boy from Brasília

To understand Kaká is to understand that he does not fit the traditional narrative of the *Jogo Bonito*. He is not a child of the *favelas*, nor did he learn his intoxicating control playing barefoot on the dusty red clay of impoverished outer cities. 

Born in Gama to a civil engineer father and a schoolteacher mother, Kaká grew up in comfortable, middle-class stability in Brasília before moving to São Paulo. He had a safety net—a rarity in a country where football is often viewed as the sole ticket out of poverty. 

"I never lacked anything," Kaká has admitted in past interviews. "That gave me the freedom to play for the love of the game, not out of desperation."

That comfortable upbringing initially earned him skepticism. But his resolve was forged not by economic hardship, but by a tragic twist of fate. At age 18, a severe diving board accident at a swimming pool resulted in a fractured vertebra. Doctors warned he might never walk again. 

Instead, Kaká made a full recovery, an experience that ignited his deeply held Evangelical Christian faith—famously displayed whenever he lifts his arms to the sky after scoring, or reveals his "I Belong to Jesus" undershirt. 

### The Triumph and Trials of São Paulo

By the time he recovered, his talent was undeniable. Emerging through the youth ranks at São Paulo FC, Kaká made an explosive senior debut in March 2001, coming off the bench to score two goals in two minutes to secure the Torneio Rio-São Paulo title against Botafogo. 

Yet, his time at the Morumbi Stadium was complicated. The demanding *Tricolor* faithful, accustomed to gritty street fighters, sometimes viewed the polished, middle-class kid with suspicion. When the team stumbled, Kaká was unfairly targeted as soft. 

When AC Milan swooped in to sign him in the summer of 2003 for a modest €8.5 million—a fee Milan owner Silvio Berlusconi later famously dubbed "peanuts"—São Paulo fans were largely resigned to his departure. They didn't realize they were watching a future legend walk out the door.

### Ancelotti’s Engine: The Tactical Apex

If São Paulo built Kaká’s foundation, it was Carlo Ancelotti’s tactical genius at Milan that unlocked his divine potential. 

When Kaká arrived in Italy, Milan’s midfield was already stacked with world-class talent, including Rui Costa and Rivaldo. But Ancelotti saw something unique in the young Brazilian: a terrifying hybrid of a classic Italian *trequartista* and a modern, high-speed vertical transitions athlete.

Ancelotti constructed his famous "Christmas Tree" (4-3-2-1) formation, placing Andrea Pirlo as the deep-lying orchestrator, backed by the industrial steel of Gennaro Gattuso and Massimo Ambrosini. This defensive cloak granted Kaká total artistic freedom behind a lone striker, usually Filippo Inzaghi or Alberto Gilardino.

Unlike traditional playmakers who demand the ball at their feet to dictate tempo, Kaká is a dynamic force of nature. He glides. His long, elegant strides devour space with deceptive speed. Under Ancelotti, Kaká became the premier counter-attacking weapon in world football—capable of receiving the ball in his own half, bursting past terrified defenders, and executing a lethal final pass or a precise finish.

Never was this tactical blueprint more devastatingly displayed than in the 2006-07 Champions League campaign. Kaká carried Milan on his shoulders, scoring 10 goals in the tournament. 

His performance against Manchester United in the semi-finals at Old Trafford was pure footballing theatre. Gliding past Sir Alex Ferguson’s defense, he effortlessly flicked the ball over Gabriel Heinze, causing Heinze and Patrice Evra to collide, before coolly slotting past Edwin van der Sar. It was a goal of unimaginable composure—a masterclass that forced the footballing world to bow down. Milan’s subsequent 2-1 revenge victory over Liverpool in the Athens final was merely the coronation.

### The Shadow of Madrid

As Kaká holds court in Paris, holding the glittering gold trophy that confirms his status as the world's best, a dark cloud of transfer speculation hovers over the San Siro. 

For over a year, Real Madrid President Ramón Calderón has openly lusted after the Brazilian. The Spanish giants, eager to usher in a new era of *Galácticos*, view Kaká as the ultimate prize—the player who can restore dominance to the Santiago Bernabéu.

For now, Kaká and Milan remain publicly united. "I have a contract until 2011, and I am happy here," Kaká stated calmly during Sunday’s ceremony. 

Yet, modern football is rarely governed by romanticism. Milan’s aging squad faces a daunting rebuild, and financial realities in Italy are beginning to pale in comparison to the vast wealth of Spain and England. Insiders whisper that Madrid is prepared to break the world transfer record to lure him to Spain. Whether Berlusconi can resist an eventual megadeal remains the multi-million-euro question hanging over European football.

### A Crown Well Deserved

For today, however, the future can wait. 2007 belongs entirely to Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite. 

In Kaká, football has found a champion who bridges the gap between old-world elegance and new-world athleticism. He is a player who plays with the joy of a child, the precision of an engineer, and the serenity of a believer. 

As Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi look on from the podium—two young men who will undoubtedly shape the next decade—it is Kaká who stands tallest. Calm, smiling, and supreme: the polite boy from Brasília who conquered the world.

---

### THE UNDISPUTED KING

With this victory, Kaká becomes the fourth Brazilian to win the award, joining the elite company of Ronaldo, Rivaldo, and Ronaldinho. 

While the football world keeps a watchful eye on the meteoric rise of runner-up Ronaldo and third-placed Messi, 2007 undeniably belongs to the graceful, elegant, and unstoppable Brazilian who conquered Europe.
